A thriving economy is dependent on a 
flourishing entrepreneurial culture, and this 
new report shines a spotlight on the vibrant 
entrepreneurial ecosystem that continues to 
grow in the West Midlands. The findings show 
that the variety of sectors, level of investment 
and size of network at play in this part of the 
country make it an increasingly important 
part of the UK economy. As a result, NatWest 
continues to grow its presence and commitment 
to supporting SMEs in the area­—but this is a 
team sport, and regional support collaboration 
and partnership are key. 
 
This report shows that the University of 
Warwick produces nearly 30% of spinout 
businesses in the West Midlands region, with 
equity raised of nearly £36m, which is why 
our recently opened Accelerator hub at the 
University is a central strand of our strategy in 
this part of the UK. It allows NatWest to support 
up-and-coming, high growth entrepreneurs 
and businesses across growing sectors such as 
interactive entertainment, deeptech and high 
value manufacturing to become future success 
stories. It also encourages future business 
owners to consider these new sectors alongside 
the more traditional, high growth sectors in this 
region such as property, automotive and food 
and drink. 
 
Our Accelerator hub is part of our wider 
network of 14 Enterprise Hubs, which is 
one of the largest of its kind across the UK 
and provides not only training and physical 
workspaces, but also coaching and access 
to peers and sector specialists. We know 
that start-ups are having to do several jobs 
at once—the CEO, Finance Director and HR 
Manager—the bank’s accelerator programme is 
designed to help them be all those things whilst 
supporting them in running their business. 
 
Over the past four years the programme has 
supported more than 3,500 individuals and 
businesses, helping them achieve an average 
turnover of £301,521 and to raise £198m in total 
investments. These hubs work in conjunction 
with our wider ambitions for the future economy 
—looking at today’s cohort, 39% of places are 
devoted to sustainability focused business, 
47% have gone to female entrepreneurs, over 
20% to ethnic minority businesses and 75% are 
outside London and the South East. 
 
What this report shows is that the many 
different businesses and sectors at play in 
the region are vital to the recovery of the UK’s 
economy. Continued collaborative working with 
all parts of the entrepreneurial ecosystem, 
including other financial institutions and 
lenders, is crucial if we are to get these funding 
structures right for entrepreneurs and start-ups. 
 
As we come out of the pandemic, and despite 
rising inflation and a cost of living crisis, 
now is a great time to start a new business 
and become an entrepreneur. There’s more 
support than ever in terms of access to grants 
and funding, networking and mentoring and 
angel investment. And as the biggest lender to 
businesses, we are determined to play our part. 
 
The team at NatWest looks forward to working 
closely with partners such as University of 
Warwick and Beauhurst to help the West 
Midlands’ future business success stories start, 
scale and thrive. 
Andrew Harrison
Managing Director, Head of NatWest Business Banking

Background
The University of Warwick has a rich history of 
supporting creativity, business partnerships 
and entrepreneurship across many disciplines. 
Warwick understands that innovation 
occurs at the intersection of customer pain 
points, fundamental research and emerging 
technologies when diverse communities, 
disciplines and talents work together in concert. 
 
To truly realise the potential, Warwick appointed 
a Chief Innovation Officer and created the 
Warwick Innovation District (WID). The 
introduction of this conductor role leading an 
Innovation Group allowed WID to build a multi-
disciplinary innovation-ecosystem well equipped 
to tackle the challenges of the future. 
 
The Warwick Innovation District has evidenced 
its capacity to address the opportunities 
available with more than 8000 people engaging 
across University talent, investors and the 
region’s businesses. Powered by the University 
of Warwick, WID has grown to become a large, 
open community that stretches from London 
where it holds Angel investor sessions to the 
University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire 
NHS Trust (UHCW), through Silicon Spa to its 
Innovation campus in Wellesbourne. WID brings 
together academics, founders and investors with 
the aim of making an impact for society and the 
West Midlands region, by launching and scaling 
businesses, and providing students with the 
opportunity to experiment and innovate. 
 
Warwick also delivers the chance for academics 
from other universities, such as Oxford, 
Birmingham, and Nottingham, to participate in the 
ICURe programme funded and run by Innovate 
UK. This incredible programme commercialises 
and accelerates research from academics, 
resulting in increased spinouts and diversity 
within WID. 
 
The specialisms within WID span a broad 
spectrum of industries, focusing on challenges 
relevant to the modern socio-economic and 
political context. One example of this is through 
the Deep Tech Innovation Centre—an incubator 
programme aimed at supporting students, 
researchers, alumni and startup companies 
working in areas including AI, Blockchain, 
Quantum Computing and Robotics. This 
programme recognises the innovation available in 
this field, and supports companies using original 
scientific and engineering research to address 
global problems. 
 
The Warwick Innovation District has also become 
engaged with challenges relating to 
sustainability, embracing this field as an industry 
rife with opportunities. The West Midlands, as 
noted in the Government’s Levelling Up White 
Paper, will be a key region for supporting the 
energy transition within the transport sector. 
In line with these findings, the Warwick 
Manufacturing Group (WMG) has partnered with 
NatWest to develop a Clean Transport Specialist 
Accelerator, which is a unique place to access 
research, test centres, support with supply chains 
and business coaching.

Top sectors by the number of high-growth companies in 
the West Midlands (2022)
In the West Midlands, the most popular sector 
for high-growth companies is property/land 
development and construction. The industry 
represents 6.77% of the region’s 2,170 active 
businesses, which is higher than the 5.73% of 
companies working in this sector across the UK. 
 
Tech companies are also well represented 
within the top sectors in Warwickshire and 
Coventry, with the sub-sectors Software–as-
a-Service (25), internet platform (19), mobile 
apps (18), and analytics, insight, tools (18) 
ranking highly by business population. These 
findings align with trends across the broader 
UK high-growth ecosystem, as tech-related 
industries have continued to grow over the last 
decade. Other key sectors in Warwickshire and 
Coventry include e-commerce (26), distribution 
(24) and property/land development and 
construction (24).

Local major employers
Jaguar Land Rover 
Headquartered in Coventry, Jaguar Land Rover is one of the most 
well-known employers in the West Midlands. The firm is a subsidiary 
of Tata Motors Ltd, formed after a 2013 merger between Jaguar 
and Land Rover to become one company. The multinational car 
manufacturer reported a turnover of £16.5b and more than 30,000 
employees across the UK in its 2021 financials. 
BT 
BT is the largest provider of fixed-line, broadband and mobile services 
in the UK. Though headquartered in London, the telecommunications 
firm employs more than 11,000 people in the West Midlands. In 2021, 
BT also opened a regional hub in Birmingham with the intention of 
creating 1,000 jobs in the city. The Three Snowhill development in 
Birmingham’s business district offers a number of amenities to staff 
and hopes to eventually be a space for 3,000 employees.
NatWest 
Incorporated in 1968, Natwest was formed through the merger of 
National Provincial Bank and Westminster Bank. It later joined the 
Royal Bank of Scotland Group, which was then renamed NatWest 
Group in 2020. The bank employs around 60,000 people in the UK. 
Natwest also runs the largest Accelerator programme in the UK 
which has supported over 30,000 entrepreneurs, including a hub at 
the University of Warwick, open to all.

Gaming
In recent years, gaming companies have become more 
prevalent within the high-growth ecosystem thanks 
to the increased array of affordable technologies and 
infrastructure, combined with more sophisticated digital 
distribution strategies and consumer demand. The West 
Midlands is a key gaming hub for the UK, with a number of 
studios calling the region home. A number of larger gaming 
companies have also opened local bases in Leamington Spa, 
including SEGA, Ubisoft, and Codemasters. Gaming markets 
continue to grow strongly and the recent launch of the 
Warwick Esports Centre has seen an important acceleration.

Digital and creative refers to companies working in digital 
media and the online publishing industry. In the West Midlands, 
there are 30 companies in this sector, ranging from content 
creators to platform-based communities. The opportunities in 
this field have been created by the dramatically reduced costs 
involved in creating and distributing digital content thanks 
to advances in visual media technology and the proliferation 
of social media networks. Businesses, such as health and 
wellbeing platform Kaido and On The Tools, which has created 
a content driven community for the construction industry, 
have capitalised on these trends by providing niche content.

Deeptech companies are those which create value via 
tangible engineering innovation or scientific advances 
and discoveries, such as Artificial Intelligence, robotics, 
blockchain, biotechnology and quantum computing. In the 
West Midlands, there are 55 companies working in this 
space, including autonomous vehicle software developer 
Eatron Technologies, optical technologist EYOTO, and 3D 
content development tool Haiper.

High-value manufacturing refers to businesses using 
knowledge-intensive techniques to produce high-
value and high-cost products. These companies range 
from small social enterprises to global giants, with 101 
businesses in this space choosing the West Midlands for 
their home location. Another firm attracted to the region is 
Lotus Cars, which is establishing an advanced technology 
centre and University partnership at the Wellesbourne 
Innovation campus. The facility will also be a base for 
Lotus’ engineering consultancy.

Medtech
Innovation is rife in the medtech field, with a large number 
of companies using the latest technological advancements 
to address medical challenges. Companies in this area 
range from those using Artificial Intelligence to expedite 
drug discovery, to others leveraging the cloud to store large 
datasets that can be shared amongst doctors. There are 
36 companies in the West Midlands working in this field, 
including portable dialysis developer Quanta, diagnostic 
specialists Creavo, and 4D Biomaterials—a company that 
creates 3D printing technology that can be used in medicine.

Emergent sectors
There are 229 high-growth companies in the West Midlands 
operating in emergent sectors. These are sectors that sit 
at the intersection of traditional sectors, such as finance 
and education, with new technologies such as automation 
and artificial intelligence. Examples include increasingly 
popular fields such as 3D printing, biofuels, challenger 
banks, edtech, gamification, robotics, smart homes, and 
urban farming. Many companies in this area are tackling 
important global problems such as how to feed a growing 
population and how to reduce inequality through education.

The number, and value, of deals invested into 
companies based in Warwickshire and Coventry 
has continued to grow over the past decade. 
Between 2012 and 2021, the value of equity 
investment quadrupled, rising from £90.9m 
to £413m. The number of deals taking place 
increased significantly, increasing from 96 
investment rounds taking place in 2012 to 208 
occurring in 2021. The largest year for equity 
growth took place between 2019 and 2020, 
when the value of fundraisings into companies 
based in the West Midlands increased by 196% 
in a single year. These results contradict the 
patterns observed in the broader high-growth 
ecosystem, where between 2019 and 2020 the 
value of equity raised dropped as a result of the 
COVID-19 pandemic. The peculiar success of 
the region during this time frame may explain 
why the number, and value, of deals taking place 
dropped between 2020 and 2021, whilst the 
broader private markets blossomed.

The top company by the value of equity 
investment secured between 2012 and 2021 
was Quanta, which develops portable dialysis 
devices that can be used for both clinical and 
home treatments. Based in Stratford-upon-
avon, the business has secured £246m of equity

accompanying valuation of £200m. 
Following Quanta, Proton Partners International 
has raised the second largest amount of equity 
investment, securing £205m between 2012 
and 2021. The company launched in 2015 and 
ran therapy centres used for cancer treatment 
prior to its exit via IPO in February 2019. Other 
companies that have raised large volumes of 
equity investment include Gymshark (£200m), 
Pritt Group (£108m), and Hayfield Homes

Considering spinouts are an opportunity for 
university researchers to commercialise their 
most innovative and valuable research, it is no 
surprise that investors are often very interested 
in this type of business. Universities with top 
research facilities and cutting-edge technology 
are likely to have more spinout companies which 
may go on to raise equity investment as they are 
able to offer these spaces for research. 
 
The regional leader of the West Midlands for 
institutions by the amount of equity raised by 
its spinouts is the University of Warwick—
these companies secured £35.8m in 2021. 
Contributing to this total was an £11.7m deal 
into Lightcast Discovery, which creates cell 
manipulation technology for drug discovery, and 
a £6.2m deal into NanoSyrinx, which develops 
nanotechnology for drug delivery to the interior 
of cells. Among all institutions across the 
whole of the UK, the University of Warwick 
ranked ninth, with the leaders being Oxford and 
Cambridge. 
 
The universities of Birmingham, Aston, and 
Coventry also have spinout companies that 
raised equity investment in 2021. Although 
spinouts from the universities of Wolverhampton 
and Keele did not secure any equity deals in 
2021, they have done so in previous years.

The Venture Centre, University of Warwick 
Based at the University of Warwick, the Venture 
Centre is designed to provide starter space for 
new tech companies, step up accommodation for 
more established businesses as well as scale up 
units in the Science Park for companies who see 
themselves requiring larger ofﬁce or lab space 
for up to 250 staff.  
 
Business Innovation Centre, Coventry 
The ofﬁce space at the Business Innovation 
Centre is a joint venture between Coventry City 
Council, Coventry & Warwickshire Chamber 
of Commerce, and the University of Warwick. 
The building was constructed aiming to allow 
companies to collaborate with these partners to 
create and foster their innovation and growth. 
 
 
Warwick Innovation Centre, Warwick 
The Warwick Innovation Centre is a prestigious 
location near to Silicon Spa for start up and small 
innovative businesses, offering purpose-designed 
accommodation on short leases. 
 
The location and connections of the Science 
Park’s innovation centres allow companies to 
access extensive business services from the 
University’s science park management as well as 
access to the Science Park’s business support 
team on application. All Innovation Centres 
have links to the University of Warwick to foster 
knowledge exchange and access vital skills. The 
Innovation Centres are also chosen by larger 
national or international firms, establishing their 
first UK office or a regional branch, bringing 
supply chains closer together.

The Innovation Campus offers businesses 
the opportunity to locate themselves in a

events and activities to support the incubation 
and acceleration of businesses on our Clean

With free hotdesking for participants and links to

Esports Centre
The Innovation Hub at the University Hospitals Coventry 
and Warwickshire NHS Trust is a specialist space designed 
to drive innovation and transformation while ensuring 
patient interests are at the forefront of their priorities. 
The space aims to achieve four key goals, with the centre 
encouraging individuals to dream, think, create and 
influence. Working in a hub built around these values 
and aspirations encourages innovation, flexibility and 
collaboration amongst users. Working in collaboration 
with the University of Warwick and the West Midlands 
Health and Wellbeing Innovation Network, they provide 
a programme of activity to create solutions to real health 
challenges with the SME community.
In response to novel research emphasising the link 
between gaming and innovation brain functions, the 
University of Warwick launched an Esports Centre that 
provides students and the local community the opportunity 
to practice, and gain, relevant skills. The Esports Centre 
hosts a series of events, including Esports Future. Funded 
by the UK Government through the UK Community 
Renewal Fund, the programme aims to implement the UK 
Government’s goals of levelling up by investing in people, 
place, and communities. This is achieved through Esports 
Futures, as participants between the ages of 16 and 24 
are taken on a two day experience where they learn a wide 
array of soft skills.

Funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority, the West 
Midlands Health & Wellbeing Innovation Network is driven 
by the University of Warwick in partnership with University 
Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust and 
Bruntwood SciTech. With the health and wellbeing of the 
nation recovering from challenging times, the network aims 
to help address real world health challenges by fostering 
and developing innovation. 
 
The programme seeks to encourage interested businesses 
and SMEs to create solutions, while the network aids their 
development with the provision of support, space, networks 
and mentoring. These partnerships will enable the creation 
and commercialisation of innovative solutions for the benefit 
of the health and economy of the region and the nation.

The Deep Tech Innovation Centre supports students, 
researchers, alumni and local startup companies to explore 
the commercial potential of their innovations in areas 
ranging from advanced materials and biotechnology to 
blockchain, quantum computing and robotics. The one 
thing they all have in common is that they are using original
